summary:
I'll skip the tool calls — I already have the notes I need. Here's the section.

I've been building keikochō, a Japanese-learning dashboard I use daily for my own hiragana practice, and this stretch was mostly about closing the gap between "the drill works" and "the drill tells you something useful." I added dated history tables so the app can say "ね was wrong 70% of the time last week, right 80% this time" instead of only tracking running totals — turns out that's harder than it sounds, because most of the state was a single JSON blob rewritten whole on every answer, so timestamped facts needed their own tables alongside it, not inside it.

The reading feature (物語, short folktales) surfaced the actual hard problem in this space: I assumed vocabulary would be the wall, but grammar is. My known-word list covers Momotarō's nouns fine, but you can't narrate a story in present-tense noun-sentences — you need past tense and verb predicates I hadn't taught yet. Worse, I found that morphological checkers don't catch invented words in all-hiragana text (a nonsense string just gets mis-segmented into two "real" looking pieces instead of flagged). The fix was to make the story generator declare every token up front and validate against that declaration, rather than trust a tokenizer to catch hallucinations after the fact.

I also added an on-demand coaching note that reads your session stats and writes a few sentences of feedback — the constraint I cared about was keeping the model from inventing anything: it only gets fed real numbers and a small vetted set of hints, and it's explicitly forbidden from naming specific Japanese words it wasn't given. Same logic run through a diagnostic feature that groups your mistakes by pattern (confused pairs, sound-alikes) — that one I built with no LLM at all, because deterministic pattern-matching on the mistake log was both cheaper and more trustworthy than asking a model to eyeball it.

Smaller thing, but the kind of bug that's satisfying to run down: on a phone, the typing drills kept jumping the page when the on-screen keyboard was open and a wrong-answer banner appeared. Two separate causes — a re-focus call that triggered iOS's auto-scroll-into-view, and a feedback message with no reserved layout space, so it shoved everything below it down. Neither was visible until I tested on an actual phone with the keyboard up.
